classification.difficultyReason: Apply the denominator restriction and solve simple quadratic equations, retaining both excluded roots; polynomial cases require no restriction.

questions.mappingNote: Every part directly assesses natural domain from an equation; parts g and h use the same quadratic-denominator restriction as Example 1(c).
questions.methodNote: The natural domain consists of allowable real inputs. Polynomials allow every real input; rational functions exclude values making the denominator zero. Example 1(a), (c) and (d) demonstrate these rules.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify unrestricted polynomial domains and exclude the zeros of linear or quadratic denominators, following Example 1.

classification.difficultyReason: Solve radicand inequalities and combine square-root validity with a nonzero denominator to distinguish strict from inclusive endpoints.

questions.mappingNote: Every part directly assesses natural domain from an equation: a–d require a non-negative radicand; e–f require a positive radicand because the square root is in the denominator.
questions.methodNote: Page 3, Example 1, requires non-negative square-root radicands and excludes zero denominators. Combine those restrictions for reciprocal square roots.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply non-negative radicand restrictions, with strict positivity when the square root is a denominator.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise unrestricted exponential and sine functions and require positive logarithmic arguments.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a, b and f use the unrestricted function families introduced on page 2. Parts c–e extend the positive logarithmic-input rule stated on page 3. The most advanced directly assessed skill is finding a natural domain from an equation.
questions.methodNote: Use the natural domain as the allowable real inputs. Pages 2–3 establish unrestricted exponential and sine domains and the positive-input restriction for logarithms. Apply that restriction to each complete logarithmic argument.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise unrestricted exponential and sine functions and require positive logarithmic arguments.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the explicitly requested vertical line test to supplied curves, recognising that zero intersections are permitted and multiple intersections fail.

questions.mappingNote: The shared instruction explicitly references Example 2. Parts a, c and d are single-valued graphs; b is a vertical line; e and h are closed curves; f and g require allowing zero intersections outside their domains; i repeats the sideways-parabola principle taught on page 4.
questions.methodNote: Pages 4–5, Example 2, test whether a vertical line x=c meets a graph at most once. Page 6 explicitly permits zero intersections. Use that graphical criterion and give a concrete vertical line with two intersections for a failing curve.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the demonstrated vertical line test to nine supplied graphs, including vertical lines and closed curves.

classification.difficultyReason: Resolve a squared relation into two straight lines, sketch both, and interpret their vertical-line intersections.

questions.mappingNote: Page 5 Example 2d explicitly resolves y²=x² into y=x or y=-x and rejects the combined graph using a vertical test line; question 5 applies the same method with gradients ±2. Pages 2 and 6 supply the unique-output definition and vertical-line criterion.
questions.methodNote: Resolve the squared relation into two linear equations, draw both lines, and apply the vertical line test. A function has at most one graph intersection with each vertical line.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Resolve a squared relation into two straight lines, sketch both, and interpret their vertical-line intersections.

classification.difficultyReason: Sketch the sideways parabola and its upper and lower branches using the supplied square-root decomposition and reflection symmetry.

questions.mappingNote: Question 6 applies the same upper/lower branch method to y²=x. Square-root graphing is the most directly assessed catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Separate a relation into its positive and negative square-root branches, sketch each branch and retain its domain. Page 4 explicitly illustrates x=y²; pages 5–6 separate a circle into upper and lower function graphs.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Sketch a sideways parabola and distinguish its upper and lower square-root branches.

classification.difficultyReason: Link routine algebraic inversion with linear graphing, swapping useful coordinates and recognising when the inverse coincides with the original line.

questions.mappingNote: Every part requires both a linear inverse and its graph, so graph-inverse-function is primary, supported by algebraic inversion and linear graphing.
questions.methodNote: Interchange x and y, then make y the subject as in Example 3a. Sketch the inverse by reflecting the original graph in y=x, swapping coordinates of useful points.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find linear inverses algebraically and sketch each reflected pair with the line y=x.

classification.difficultyReason: Rearrange cubic and reciprocal rules, then translate algebra into reflected curve shapes, key points and exchanged horizontal and vertical asymptotes.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a, b, c and e extend the cubic example; d, f, g and h use the stated general inverse procedure on translated reciprocals. Graph-inverse-function captures the most advanced directly requested task.
questions.methodNote: Example 3b interchanges variables and takes a cube root. The preceding teaching shows that inverse graphs exchange coordinates and reflect in y=x. Apply the same variable interchange to reciprocal equations, with reflected asymptotes.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Invert cubic and translated reciprocal functions, then sketch reflected curves with appropriate intercepts and asymptotes.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute numerical inputs into a linear rule and combine function values.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts directly assess evaluation in function notation; d–f add arithmetic with the resulting values.
questions.methodNote: Substitute the input for every occurrence of x, evaluate, then combine function values as instructed; Example 4 demonstrates numerical substitution.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute numerical inputs into a linear rule and combine function values.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate a quadratic rule at integer, fractional and surd inputs.

questions.mappingNote: This question uses the same substitution method with fractional and surd inputs and a sum of values.
questions.methodNote: Example 4 substitutes into a squared input, retaining parentheses for negative inputs.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate a quadratic rule at integer, fractional and surd inputs.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute each supplied input into both occurrences of x, preserve subtraction signs and simplify the resulting numerical quotient.

questions.mappingNote: Every requested input is allowable; the assessed task is numerical evaluation rather than determining a domain.
questions.methodNote: Substitute the input throughout the rule as in Example 4; preserve numerator and denominator grouping. Page 3 establishes that denominators cannot be zero.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute signed and fractional inputs into a rational function and simplify exactly.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate output statements into reciprocal equations and solve for the input; the final part first requires interpreting and evaluating f(-2).

questions.mappingNote: The question asks for inputs from specified outputs, so solve-function-equation is the closest skill. The supplied teaching pages do not demonstrate the equation-solving steps themselves.
questions.methodNote: Function notation denotes the output of the given rule; substitute the reciprocal expression and solve the resulting equation, excluding x=0.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Replace function notation with a reciprocal rule and solve for its input.

classification.difficultyReason: Solve quadratic function equations, including repeated roots, irrational roots and no real solution.

questions.mappingNote: The most advanced assessed task is solving for function inputs. The supplied pages establish function notation and quadratic ranges but do not explicitly teach factorisation or completing the square.
questions.methodNote: Interpret function notation using page 11 and equate the quadratic rule to the required output. Use factorisation or completing the square to solve.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Solve quadratic function equations, including repeated roots, irrational roots and no real solution.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute algebraic arguments and expand squared binomials or simplify powers.

questions.mappingNote: Every part evaluates an algebraic argument; b and d require binomial expansion, matching Example 4's demonstrated process.
questions.methodNote: Example 4 substitutes algebraic arguments into a quadratic rule, uses parentheses, expands the square and collects terms.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute algebraic arguments and expand squared binomials or simplify powers.

classification.difficultyReason: Distinguish numerical equalities from general algebraic identities by substitution and expansion.

questions.mappingNote: Numerical checks support a–b; algebraic substitution establishes d–f and reveals the extra cross term in c. No written justification is requested from students, so each response is an inline true/false cloze.
questions.methodNote: Use f(x)=x² by substituting the entire input, then expand and simplify as in Example 4. Compare both sides of each statement.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Distinguish numerical equalities from general algebraic identities by substitution and expansion.

classification.difficultyReason: Compare numerical and algebraic substitutions to distinguish valid identities from false statements.

questions.mappingNote: Each statement requires substituting its argument into g(t)=3t and comparing the two sides. Unequal evaluations provide counterexamples for false universal statements.
questions.methodNote: Page 11 introduces function notation and evaluates numerical and algebraic arguments by substitution; Example 4 substitutes expressions into the function rule.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Compare numerical and algebraic substitutions to distinguish valid identities from false statements.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine an output reflection with a vertical translation, simplify the resulting linear rule and locate points or intercepts for its sketch.

questions.mappingNote: Reflection is directly assessed in c and d, together with linear graphing and translation.
questions.methodNote: Use vertical translations and reflection in the x-axis; locate intercepts to sketch each line.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Sketch a linear rule and its vertical translations and reflections.

classification.difficultyReason: Distinguish input and output negation, apply both to the linear rule and recognise that the double reflection reproduces the original graph.

questions.mappingNote: Part d assesses successive reflections, making reflect-function-graphs the primary skill.
questions.methodNote: Apply vertical translation, reflection in the x-axis and reflection in the y-axis to a known graph.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Includes a double reflection of a line through the origin.

classification.difficultyReason: Coordinate transformations with sketches and domain-range statements across three function families, especially reflecting the logarithm in both axes and tracking its allowed inputs and asymptotic direction.

questions.mappingNote: Combined transformations across function families, particularly both reflections in i, are the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Start with the standard parabola, exponential or logarithm; translate and reflect as in Examples 8 and 10, then read the domain and range from the graph.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply transformations across quadratic, exponential and logarithmic families and infer domains and ranges.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires completing the square or combining square-root translations and reflection, then linking vertices or endpoints and graph direction to domain and range. These are routine linked applications of taught graph methods.

questions.mappingNote: The square-root family is the most advanced family assessed in four of six parts; quadratic sketching and combined transformations are secondary.
questions.methodNote: Use standard graph shapes, vertex form, transformations, radicand restrictions and graph extrema; Example 9 models graphing before reading the range.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Sketch quadratic and square-root functions, including translated and reflected roots, and state their domains and ranges.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise a semicircle and compare its translation and reflection on shared axes.

questions.mappingNote: Recognition and sketching of semicircles is central; transformations supply the two additional curves.
questions.methodNote: Identify the upper semicircle from its circle equation, then translate vertically and reflect in the x-axis.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise a semicircle and compare its translation and reflection on shared axes.

classification.difficultyReason: Factor a cubic to locate its zeros and compare reflected and vertically dilated curves.

questions.mappingNote: The factor -2 requires reflection and dilation, with dilation the most advanced directly assessed transformation.
questions.methodNote: Use the cubic shape and intercepts, reflection in the x-axis, then the vertical stretch of Example 11; no calculus is required.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Factor a cubic to locate its zeros and compare reflected and vertically dilated curves.

classification.difficultyReason: Compare four reciprocal curves using vertical dilation and reflection on shared axes.

questions.mappingNote: The two factor-2 curves explicitly assess vertical dilation of a known hyperbola.
questions.methodNote: Use the reciprocal graph, multiply ordinates for vertical stretches and reflect in the x-axis for negative multipliers.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Compare four reciprocal curves using vertical dilation and reflection on shared axes.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate two successive linear rules and interpret their combined translation.

questions.mappingNote: The question directly assesses numerical and algebraic compositions of linear functions, followed by interpreting the successive subtraction and addition as translations along a line.
questions.methodNote: Evaluate the inner function first, then substitute its output into the outer function. Page 18 introduces numerical and algebraic composition; Example 12 on page 19 demonstrates successive substitution.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate two successive linear rules and interpret their combined translation.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate nested functions, simplify polynomial composites and compare composition orders.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–f evaluate numerical composites; g–j derive composite rules; k compares the two orders. Determining composite equations is the most advanced directly assessed catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Evaluate the inner function first, then substitute its output into the outer function. For algebraic inputs, substitute the complete expression and expand and simplify, following Example 12. Composition order can produce different functions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate nested functions, simplify polynomial composites and compare composition orders.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate numerical and algebraic composites in both orders, then recognise inverse functions.

questions.mappingNote: Page 18 introduces composition; page 19 Example 12 demonstrates numerical and algebraic substitution and defines inverse pairs through both compositions; page 20 Example 13 verifies inverses using this criterion. Question 3 directly assesses that criterion.
questions.methodNote: Evaluate the inner function first, then substitute its output into the outer function. For algebraic composites substitute the complete expression and simplify. Identify inverses by obtaining x in both composition orders.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate numerical and algebraic composites in both orders, then recognise inverse functions.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate rational composites, simplify both algebraic compositions and recognise inverse functions.

questions.mappingNote: The concluding relationship requires inverse verification using the two algebraic compositions, making verify-inverse-composition the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Evaluate the inner function first, substitute its output into the outer function and simplify. Example 12 includes rational compositions and their domains. The inverse definition and Example 13 verify inverses by showing both compositions equal the input.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate rational composites, simplify both algebraic compositions and recognise inverse functions.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires interchanging variables, rearranging a linear rule and plotting the function and inverse consistently as reflections in y=x. The sequence is directly modelled; repeated parts and fractional coefficients add no new conceptual demand.

questions.mappingNote: All five parts repeat Example 14 with linear functions. Graphing the inverse is the most advanced directly assessed skill; finding its rule is also required.
questions.methodNote: Page 20 Example 14 directly teaches interchanging x and y, making y the subject, and drawing the function and inverse as reflections in y=x on common axes.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Rearrange five linear rules to obtain inverses and sketch each function, its inverse and the reflection line on common axes.

classification.difficultyReason: Interchange the variables and isolate the inverse using cube or fifth roots.

questions.mappingNote: All three parts directly assess finding an inverse algebraically. Odd roots give a single real inverse without a domain restriction.
questions.methodNote: Example 14 interchanges x and y and makes y the subject. Example 13 establishes the cube-root inverse of a cubic, and Example 15 applies the interchange method to a translated cubic.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Interchange the variables and isolate the inverse using cube or fifth roots.

classification.difficultyReason: Rearrange rational functions after interchanging variables and identify excluded inputs for both functions.

questions.mappingNote: Part a reverses a translated reciprocal; part b directly parallels Example 16 with a different translation. Parts c and d extend the same inverse procedure by collecting terms containing y. Finding inverse rules is the primary assessed skill; both domain requirements are retained.
questions.methodNote: Exclude zero denominators. Following Example 16, interchange x and y, make y the subject, and exclude zero denominators in the inverse. The sign errors in Example 16's printed domain and range statements are not carried into these answers.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Rearrange rational functions after interchanging variables and identify excluded inputs for both functions.

classification.difficultyReason: Verify self-inverse functions by composition, including simplifying compound rational expressions.

questions.mappingNote: Every part directly assesses verification of an inverse by composition; parts e and f require compound-fraction simplification. No supplied teaching demonstration is reproduced as practice.
questions.methodNote: Example 13 and the Composite and inverse summary establish verification by composition. For a self-inverse function, substituting the function into itself gives x. Denominator restrictions follow the natural-domain teaching.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Verify self-inverse functions by composition, including simplifying compound rational expressions.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires reversing shifts and scale factors using exponential-logarithmic equivalence, then determining natural domains from positive logarithm arguments. The hardest parts link several familiar inverse operations with a shifted domain restriction.

questions.mappingNote: Every part directly assesses finding an inverse rule and both natural domains. Part a is linear; b, c, g and i invert exponential rules; d, e, f and h invert logarithmic rules. Example 16 supplies the domain-and-inverse sequence; page 3 supplies the logarithmic domain restriction.
questions.methodNote: Interchange x and y and make y the subject, as in Examples 14–16. Require positive logarithm arguments; the inverse domain equals the original range.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Rearrange linear, exponential and logarithmic rules to find inverses, retaining the natural domains of both functions.

classification.difficultyReason: Divide a relation into restricted functions and justify that each restriction has an inverse.

questions.mappingNote: Page 5 develops semicircle functions from a circle. Pages 21–22 explain the horizontal line test and its relationship to reflection and the vertical line test. The task directly assesses restrictions that produce invertible functions.
questions.methodNote: Split a circle into upper and lower square-root functions, then restrict each to a quadrant. Apply the vertical line test for a function and the horizontal line test for an inverse.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Divide a relation into restricted functions and justify that each restriction has an inverse.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the standard restrictions on denominators and square-root radicands to familiar functions.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and f use unrestricted polynomial domains; b, c, d and g exclude their denominator zeros; e and h solve non-negative-radicand inequalities. All eight directly assess natural domain from an equation.
questions.methodNote: The natural domain consists of allowable real inputs. Example 1 excludes zero denominators and requires square-root radicands to be non-negative; polynomial inputs are unrestricted.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the standard restrictions on denominators and square-root radicands to familiar functions.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute numerical and algebraic arguments into a quadratic function, including expanding a squared binomial.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–d evaluate numerical inputs; e–h evaluate algebraic inputs. The most advanced assessed operation is substitution of a compound algebraic argument and expansion, matching evaluate-function-algebraic-argument.
questions.methodNote: Substitute the entire argument for x, bracket negative or compound arguments, then square and simplify. Example 4 demonstrates numerical substitution, a doubled algebraic argument and expansion of a squared binomial.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute numerical and algebraic arguments into a quadratic function, including expanding a squared binomial.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute numerical and simple algebraic arguments into a linear function, including distributing a negative coefficient.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–d evaluate numerical inputs; parts e–h evaluate algebraic arguments. The compound argument in h requires distribution, making algebraic-argument evaluation the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Substitute the complete argument for x, use parentheses for negative or compound arguments, then simplify. Example 4 demonstrates numerical and algebraic substitutions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute numerical and simple algebraic arguments into a linear function, including distributing a negative coefficient.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify allowable inputs and outputs for linear, quadratic and reciprocal functions.

questions.mappingNote: Part a uses an unrestricted nonconstant straight line; part b repeats the exact function in page 12 Example 5 and its maximum-value argument; part c applies the reciprocal graph from page 2 with its excluded input shifted to -6. The question directly assesses both domain and range.
questions.methodNote: Determine the natural domain from allowable inputs, excluding zero denominators. Determine the range from familiar graph features, as taught on page 12.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify allowable inputs and outputs for linear, quadratic and reciprocal functions.

classification.difficultyReason: Sketch a given linear function after reflection, vertical translations and a vertical dilation.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–d apply these rules separately to h(x)=4x+2. The dilation in d is the most advanced directly assessed transformation; reflection, translation and straight-line graphing are secondary.
questions.methodNote: Page 14 defines vertical translation, page 15 defines reflection in the x-axis, and page 17 defines stretching from the x-axis by multiplying ordinates.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Sketch a given linear function after reflection, vertical translations and a vertical dilation.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires sketching a familiar parabola and directly applying the supplied reflection and vertical-translation forms, keeping the three vertices and opening directions consistent on shared axes.

questions.mappingNote: Apply these transformations to the given quadratic without separating the three requested curves into independent response parts.
questions.methodNote: Page 14 teaches that adding a constant translates a graph vertically. Page 15 teaches reflection in the x-axis for y=-f(x), including the coordinate mapping (a,b) to (a,-b).

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Compare a parabola, its reflection in the x-axis and its vertical translation on shared axes.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate numerical composites, expand algebraic composites including a quartic, and compare composition orders.

questions.mappingNote: Page 11 Example 4 teaches numerical and algebraic substitution and expansion. Page 19 Example 12 directly demonstrates numerical and algebraic composites; its preceding note shows that reversing composition order generally changes the result. Forming the algebraic composite rules is the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Evaluate the inner function first and substitute its result into the outer function. For algebraic arguments substitute the complete expression in brackets, then expand and simplify. Compare composition orders using their expressions or a counterexample.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate numerical composites, expand algebraic composites including a quartic, and compare composition orders.

classification.difficultyReason: Interchange variables and rearrange linear, cubic and reciprocal rules.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and b directly apply Example 14's linear rearrangement. Part c applies Example 15's cubic inverse method. Part d uses the same variable interchange with reciprocal rearrangement and the nonzero-denominator restriction. All four directly assess finding inverse functions.
questions.methodNote: Page 20 Example 14 interchanges x and y and rearranges to find an inverse. Page 21 Example 15 applies the same method to a shifted cubic, taking a cube root. Pages 2–3 explain exclusions caused by zero denominators.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Interchange variables and rearrange linear, cubic and reciprocal rules.

classification.difficultyReason: Establishes identities and inequalities for arbitrary real inputs by comparing symbolic function values.

questions.mappingNote: The assessed task is symbolic evaluation and proof of identities for arbitrary inputs, rather than graphing or composition.
questions.methodNote: Substitute the complete algebraic argument into the function rule, expand and compare expressions. Page 11 demonstrates substitution of algebraic arguments; pages 18–19 reinforce function evaluation and symbolic substitution.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Establishes identities and inequalities for arbitrary real inputs by comparing symbolic function values.

classification.difficultyReason: Proves an identity for arbitrary real inputs and determines every whole-number pair satisfying a functional equation.

questions.mappingNote: The task compares evaluation at an algebraic argument with a product of function values. Pages 18–19 distinguish composition from ordinary multiplication; this question assesses multiplication, not composition.
questions.methodNote: Use substitution into the function rule, as demonstrated on page 11. Apply the product index law in part a; in part b substitute first, then solve the resulting integer equation and check the pairs.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Proves an identity for arbitrary real inputs and determines every whole-number pair satisfying a functional equation.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires constructing general symbolic proofs from the supplied parity definitions. The hardest part applies oddness first inside a composition and then to the outer function at the argument g(x), with earlier sum and product proofs providing scaffolding.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–d apply the definitions directly to examples, sums and products; part e applies oddness first to the inner function and then to the outer function. The most advanced directly assessed skill is proving parity properties.
questions.methodNote: Use substitution in function notation, the embedded even/odd definitions, and the composition convention that the inner function is evaluated first.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires general proofs about sums, products and compositions using the definitions of even and odd functions.

existingTransferReview.note: Decision 2 (James, 11 November 2026): published on the recorded review covering each question's current content; no new model review.

bankProjection.note: Source-confirmed category headings are omitted only from bank prompts and presentation. Explicit equivalent fraction notation repairs satisfy bank validation. Source booklet content and all questions are retained.
